questions.q: What is the orbital velocity of a satellite in a circular orbit just above Earth's surface (h ≈ 0)? Express in terms of g and R_E, and give the numerical value using g = 9.8 m/s², R_E = 6400 km.
questions.a: v₀ = √(gR_E) = √(9.8 × 6.4×10⁶) ≈ 7920 m/s ≈ 7.92 km/s. A wrong answer like v = √(2gR_E) reveals confusion with escape velocity; v = gR_E reveals dimensional inconsistency (m²/s² vs m/s); forgetting to convert km to m reveals unit negligence.

questions.q: A student claims: "If we double the altitude of a satellite, its orbital velocity becomes half." Is this correct? Explain why or why not using the formula v = √(GM_E/(R_E+h)).
questions.a: Incorrect. Velocity varies as 1/√r, not 1/r. Doubling altitude means r changes from R_E to R_E+2h, not 2R_E. Even if h=0, doubling r gives v_new = v₀/√2 ≈ 0.707v₀, not v₀/2. A student saying "yes" confuses inverse proportionality with inverse square root proportionality and ignores that altitude is added to R_E, not multiplied.

questions.q: Calculate the orbital period of a satellite at height h = 400 km above Earth's surface. Given: G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², M_E = 6.0×10²⁴ kg, R_E = 6400 km. Show all unit conversions.
questions.a: r = 6400 + 400 = 6800 km = 6.8×10⁶ m. T = 2π√(r³/GM_E) = 2π√((6.8×10⁶)³/(6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 6.0×10²⁴)) = 2π√(3.14×10²⁰/4.0×10¹⁴) = 2π√(7.85×10⁵) = 2π × 886 ≈ 5567 s ≈ 92.8 minutes. Wrong answer 5567 s without converting to minutes shows incomplete interpretation; using h instead of r shows misunderstanding of orbital radius.

questions.q: Two satellites A and B orbit Earth in circular orbits. Satellite A is at altitude h_A = 200 km, satellite B at h_B = 800 km. Compare their orbital velocities and periods. Which satellite has greater angular momentum per unit mass (L/m = vr)? Justify without calculating exact values.
questions.a: v_A > v_B because v ∝ 1/√r and r_A < r_B. T_A < T_B because T ∝ r^(3/2). Angular momentum per unit mass L/m = vr = √(GM_E r), so L/m increases with r. Thus satellite B has greater L/m despite lower speed. A student claiming A has greater L/m because it's faster ignores that r is larger for B and L/m ∝ √r.

questions.q: A proposed solution states: "For a satellite at height h, T = 2π√((R_E+h)/g) because g' = g(R_E/(R_E+h))² and T = 2π√(r/g')." Identify the error and give the correct expression.
questions.a: The error: using g' (gravity at altitude) in T = 2π√(r/g') is dimensionally correct but physically wrong — this formula is for a simple pendulum, not orbital motion. Correct: T = 2π√(r³/GM_E) = 2π√(r²/g') = 2π√((R_E+h)³/GM_E). The student confused the centripetal acceleration v²/r = g' with the pendulum formula. Correct derivation: g' = GM_E/r², v = √(g'r), T = 2πr/v = 2π√(r/g') — wait, this actually gives the same result! Let me recheck: v²/r = GM_E/r² = g', so v = √(g'r), T = 2πr/√(g'r) = 2π√(r/g'). So T = 2π√(r/g') IS correct! The error is in the student's expression: they wrote T = 2π√((R_E+h)/g) using surface g, not g'. The correct form with g is T = 2π√((R_E+h)³/(gR_E²)). A student missing the cube and R_E² reveals algebraic manipulation error.

questions.q: Design a thought experiment to determine Earth's mass M_E using only measurements of a satellite's orbital period T and orbital radius r (measured from Earth's centre). Explain the steps and the formula you would use.
questions.a: Measure T (e.g., by timing successive passes overhead) and r (e.g., by radar ranging). Use Kepler's third law derived from Newton's gravitation: T² = 4π²r³/(GM_E). Rearrange: M_E = 4π²r³/(GT²). This is how Cavendish "weighed the Earth" using the Moon's orbit. A poor answer uses g = GM_E/R_E² (requires knowing g and R_E separately) or suggests measuring force directly (impossible for distant satellite).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Orbital velocity is the minimum horizontal velocity required for a satellite to maintain a stable circular orbit around Earth at a given altitude, where the ______ force provides exactly the required centripetal force.
Fill in the blank: Watch a video of the International Space Station passing ______ — it moves at about 7.7 km/s at 400 km altitude.
What is Orbital velocity? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Orbital velocity is the minimum horizontal velocity required for a satellite to maintain a stable circular orbit around Earth at a given altitude, where the gravitational force provides exactly the required centripetal force.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: For a satellite of mass m in circular orbit at distance r = R_E + h from Earth's centre (R_E = Earth's radius, h = altitude), orbital velocity v = √(GM_E/r) and period T = ______π√(r³/GM_E), where M_E is Earth's mass and G is the gravitational constant.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Orbital velocity?
questions.a: Students believe orbital velocity is constant for all satellites regardless of altitude because "space has no gravity" or "satellites float." They confuse the sensation of weightlessness (free fall) with absence of gravitational force.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can calculate orbital velocity and period for any given satellite altitude using v = √(GM_E/(R_E+h)) and T = 2π√((R_E+h)³/GM_E), can derive the relation T² ∝ (R_E+h)³ from force balance, and can explain why orbital velocity decreases with altitude while period increases.
